explanations.answer: To go fight for it with him
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Ahab, king of Israel, asks Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, “Will you go with me to fight against Ramoth-gilead?” (1 Kings 22:4). He had just told his servants the city was theirs, and now he turns to his guest with a job. Most hosts show you the guest room. Ahab shows you the battlefield.

explanations.answer: To pay Aram a price for it
explanations.explanation: There's no money in this scene. Ahab, king of Israel, told his servants they hadn't taken the city from the king of Aram, and then he asked Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, “Will you go with me to fight against Ramoth-gilead?” (1 Kings 22:4). So his plan is a battle, not a bargain. Nobody is haggling at a yard sale here.

explanations.answer: To ask Aram's king to give it up
explanations.explanation: Ahab doesn't ask Aram's king anything. He asks the guest in front of him, Jehoshaphat, king of Judah: “Will you go with me to fight against Ramoth-gilead?” (1 Kings 22:4). It's a request to fight, not a request to hand it over. Nobody is writing a polite letter in this story, friend.

Not quite, friend. Jehoshaphat gives Ahab the opposite of a no: “I am as you are, my people are your people, and my horses are your horses.” (1 Kings 22:4). Judah's king puts his people and his horses on the table. That's a man saying yes with his whole stable.

Right, it's false. Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, answers Ahab, “I am as you are, my people are your people, and my horses are your horses.” (1 Kings 22:4). He doesn't turn Ahab down. He puts his people and his horses in. Even the horses got signed up without a vote.

explanations.answer: Go up and the Lord will give him the city
explanations.explanation: That's it. About four hundred prophets tell Ahab, “Go up,” and add, “and the Lord will deliver it into the hand of the king.” (1 Kings 22:6). Four hundred men, and not one of them says stay home. That's a whole room singing the same note.

explanations.answer: Stay home and leave the city to Aram
explanations.explanation: Nobody there says stay home. The prophets tell Ahab, “Go up,” and “…the Lord will deliver it into the hand of the king.” (1 Kings 22:6). Ahab asked if he should go or refrain, and the answer was go. Not one voice picked the couch.

explanations.answer: Wait until Judah's army grows bigger
explanations.explanation: No waiting is mentioned. The prophets say, “Go up,” and “…the Lord will deliver it into the hand of the king.” (1 Kings 22:6). Ahab asked go or refrain, and they answered go. In this verse, nobody asks for more time or a bigger army.

Yes, friend. Jehoshaphat asks, “Is there not still a prophet of the LORD here of whom we can inquire?” (1 Kings 22:7). Four hundred prophets just said go, and he still wants to ask one more. I think four hundred yeses didn't settle it for him.

It's true, and that's the surprise. Right after the four hundred prophets say go, Jehoshaphat asks, “Is there not still a prophet of the LORD here of whom we can inquire?” (1 Kings 22:7). He keeps asking after the whole room has answered. I think four hundred yeses weren't enough for him.

Yes. Ahab says Micaiah “…never prophesies anything good for me, but only bad.” (1 Kings 22:8). The reason he gives is the kind of news Micaiah brings. That's like being mad at the oven timer for going off.

Ahab never says Micaiah is untrue. His complaint is that Micaiah “…never prophesies anything good for me, but only bad.” (1 Kings 22:8). The reason he gives is the kind of news, good or bad. Truth doesn't come up in what he says.

Ahab doesn't call Micaiah unclear. He says Micaiah “…never prophesies anything good for me, but only bad.” (1 Kings 22:8). So the complaint is about good and bad news, not about confusing words. If anything, Ahab understands Micaiah just fine.

That's right. After Jehoshaphat says, “The king should not say that!” Ahab calls one of his officials and says, “Bring Micaiah son of Imlah at once.” (1 Kings 22:9). He says at once, friend. Ahab hates the man and still sends for him fast.

It's true. Ahab calls one of his officials and says, “Bring Micaiah son of Imlah at once.” (1 Kings 22:9). He doesn't argue or drag his feet. He sends for the man he just said he hates, and he wants him fast.

Yes. Zedekiah, son of Chenaanah, says the LORD declares, “With these you shall gore the Arameans until they are finished off.” (1 Kings 22:11). The king of Aram is the one Ahab says he hasn't taken Ramoth-gilead from. Zedekiah brings a prop for the point he's making.

Philistines aren't in this scene. Zedekiah, son of Chenaanah, says, “With these you shall gore the Arameans until they are finished off.” (1 Kings 22:11). The Arameans are the people of the king Ahab says he hasn't taken the city from. Zedekiah's iron horns come with a message about Aram.

Moabites don't come up here. Zedekiah, son of Chenaanah, says, “With these you shall gore the Arameans until they are finished off.” (1 Kings 22:11). That fits, because Aram's king holds the city Ahab wants. Zedekiah's whole show is aimed at Aram.

explanations.answer: Speak favorably like the other prophets
explanations.explanation: Yes. The messenger tells Micaiah, “Behold now, with one accord the words of the prophets are favorable to the king. So please let your words be like theirs, and speak favorably.” (1 Kings 22:13). He's asking Micaiah to match the other prophets. That's a lot of pressure to put on one man.

explanations.answer: Tell the king to stay home this time
explanations.explanation: The messenger pushes the other way. He says, “Behold now, with one accord the words of the prophets are favorable to the king. So please let your words be like theirs, and speak favorably.” (1 Kings 22:13). The messenger wants Micaiah to match the other prophets, and they all said go. Telling the king to stay home would break from them.

explanations.answer: Say nothing at all in front of the kings
explanations.explanation: The messenger doesn't ask for silence. He says, “So please let your words be like theirs, and speak favorably.” (1 Kings 22:13). He wants Micaiah to speak, and to sound like the other prophets. He's asking Micaiah to sing along, not sit the song out.

Yes, friend. Micaiah answers, “As surely as the LORD lives, I will speak whatever the LORD tells me.” (1 Kings 22:14). That's his answer to a messenger who just asked him to match four hundred prophets. He doesn't promise to match the room. He promises to speak what the LORD tells him.

It's true. Micaiah says, “As surely as the LORD lives, I will speak whatever the LORD tells me.” (1 Kings 22:14). That's his answer to the messenger's request to speak favorably. His promise is about what the LORD tells him, not about what the room wants.

Yes, and it surprises you, doesn't it? Micaiah says, “Go up and triumph…” and adds, “…for the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king.” (1 Kings 22:15). That sounds just like the other prophets. I think Ahab's very next words show he wasn't buying it.

Micaiah doesn't ask for more time. He says, “Go up and triumph…” and adds, “…for the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king.” (1 Kings 22:15). That's the same message as the four hundred prophets. Hold on to that, because Ahab clearly isn't done with him.

Peace with Aram isn't what Micaiah says first. He says, “Go up and triumph…” and adds, “…for the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king.” (1 Kings 22:15). It's the message the others gave. I think Ahab hears something in it, because he answers right away.

Not quite, friend. Ahab doesn't take it at Micaiah's word. He answers, “How many times must I make you swear not to tell me anything but the truth in the name of the LORD?” (1 Kings 22:16). Ahab had the news he wanted and still pushed back.

Right, it's false. Ahab hears Micaiah say go up and triumph, and he answers, “How many times must I make you swear not to tell me anything but the truth in the name of the LORD?” (1 Kings 22:16). He doesn't take it at Micaiah's word. He pushes for something more.

That's the one. The LORD says, “These people have no master; let each one return home in peace.” (1 Kings 22:17). Sheep without a shepherd, people without a master. Both pictures show someone missing at the top.
A home is what they're sent to. The LORD says, “These people have no master; let each one return home in peace.” (1 Kings 22:17). The people have a home to go back to. What's missing is a master.

The LORD doesn't mention prophets there. He says, “These people have no master; let each one return home in peace.” (1 Kings 22:17). The word is master, like the shepherd in the picture. Funny enough, prophets are all over this scene.
Yes. Ahab says to Jehoshaphat, “Did I not tell you that he never prophesies good for me, but only bad?” (1 Kings 22:18). He's counting it as proof. He turns to Jehoshaphat like the case is closed.

It's true. Ahab turns to Jehoshaphat and says, “Did I not tell you that he never prophesies good for me, but only bad?” (1 Kings 22:18). He treats what Micaiah just said as proof of what he told Jehoshaphat earlier. Ahab is pointing at Micaiah like the case is closed.

explanations.answer: Who will entice Ahab to fall at Ramoth-gilead
explanations.explanation: Yes. Micaiah says he saw the LORD ask, “Who will entice Ahab to march up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?” (1 Kings 22:20). It's a heavy scene, so I'll keep my jokes in the oven. Notice that the question is about Ahab and Ramoth-gilead, the very city he wants.

explanations.answer: Who will warn Ahab to stay out of the war
explanations.explanation: That's not the question in Micaiah's vision. He says the LORD asks, “Who will entice Ahab to march up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?” (1 Kings 22:20). It's about enticing Ahab to march up, not warning him off. This is a heavy part, friend, so it's worth reading slowly.

explanations.answer: Who will fight for Israel at Ramoth-gilead
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't ask for a fighter. Micaiah says He asks, “Who will entice Ahab to march up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?” (1 Kings 22:20). The question is about Ahab and what happens to him. It's a heavy part, so I'll just say it plainly.

Yes. The spirit says, “I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.” (1 Kings 22:22). That's the first blank. The word is lying, and it explains why Micaiah is telling Ahab something different from the four hundred.

That's the second blank. The spirit says, “I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.” (1 Kings 22:22). These are the same prophets who all said go up. Micaiah is pulling back the curtain on the whole room.

Faithful is the opposite of what the spirit says. He says, “I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.” (1 Kings 22:22). The spirit says lying, not faithful. That one word is the whole story.

The spirit doesn't say soldiers. He says, “I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.” (1 Kings 22:22). The mouths in question belong to the prophets. Soldiers aren't named in that line.

Servants are in this chapter, but not in this verse. Ahab spoke to his servants back in verse 3, and here the spirit says, “I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.” (1 Kings 22:22). The mouths in question belong to prophets. That's the word that fits the blank.

Yes. The LORD says to the spirit, “You will surely entice him and prevail... Go and do it.” (1 Kings 22:22). It's a heavy moment in the vision, so I'll just let the words stand. Micaiah tells Ahab this in the open, in front of both kings.

It's true. The LORD says, “You will surely entice him and prevail…” and adds, “Go and do it.” (1 Kings 22:22). Micaiah describes that to Ahab straight, with both kings listening. It's a heavy part, so I'll just let the words stand.

explanations.answer: He'll see on the day he hides in an inner room
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Micaiah answers Zedekiah, “You will soon see, on that day when you go and hide in an inner room.” (1 Kings 22:25). Zedekiah had just struck him in the face, and this is his answer. He doesn't say what that day will look like, and I won't guess.

explanations.answer: He'll see on the day Ramoth-gilead falls to Israel
explanations.explanation: Micaiah doesn't mention Ramoth-gilead in his answer. He says, “You will soon see, on that day when you go and hide in an inner room.” (1 Kings 22:25). The day he points to is about Zedekiah hiding. Zedekiah had just struck him in the face, and that's the answer he gives.

explanations.answer: He'll see on the day the king sends him away
explanations.explanation: The king does send Micaiah away next, but that's not the day Micaiah names. He says, “You will soon see, on that day when you go and hide in an inner room.” (1 Kings 22:25). Micaiah is talking about what Zedekiah will do. Zedekiah had struck him in the face, and this is the word he gives back.

explanations.answer: Put him in prison until Ahab returns
explanations.explanation: Yes. Ahab says, “Put this man in prison and feed him only bread and water until I return safely.” (1 Kings 22:27). Ahab's order has an end date in it, and it's his own safe return. The order also says to feed Micaiah only bread and water.

explanations.answer: Let him go home to his father Imlah
explanations.explanation: Ahab isn't sending him home. He says, “Put this man in prison and feed him only bread and water until I return safely.” (1 Kings 22:27). Micaiah is called the son of Imlah in this chapter, but there's no trip home in the order. The order is prison, with bread and water.

explanations.answer: Guard him at the gate until the battle
explanations.explanation: There's no gate duty in Ahab's order. He says, “Put this man in prison and feed him only bread and water until I return safely.” (1 Kings 22:27). Ahab orders prison, and he names his own safe return as the end of it. A guard at the gate would've been a much nicer spot.

Yes. Micaiah says, “If you ever return safely, the LORD has not spoken through me.” (1 Kings 22:28). He says it right after the king orders him to prison. He puts the whole test on one thing: whether Ahab returns safely.

It's true. Micaiah says, “If you ever return safely, the LORD has not spoken through me.” (1 Kings 22:28). That's his answer to being sent to prison. He ties everything he said to that one test, and it's out in the open for everyone to hear.
